messages.content: What are the different properties of Hydrogen?

function.name: look_up_scientific_contributions
function.description: Look up major contributions of a particular scientist, based on their name. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

contributions.description: The number of major contributions to return, defaults to 3 if not provided.

**Hydrogen – Key Physical & Chemical Properties** | Property | Value / Description | |----------|---------------------| | **Atomic number** | 1 | | **Symbol** | H | | **Atomic mass** | 1.008 u (average) | | **Electron configuration** | 1s¹ | | **Isotopes** | Protium (¹H, 99.98 %), Deuterium (²H, 0.02 %) – stable; Tritium (³H) – radioactive (half‑life ≈12.32 y) | | **State at STP** | Colorless, odorless, tasteless gas | | **Density** | 0.08988 g L⁻¹ (at 0 °C, 1 atm) | | **Molar volume** | 22.414 L mol⁻¹ | | **Melting point** | –259.16 °C (−434.3 °F) | | **Boiling point** | –252.87 °C (–423.17 °F) | | **Specific heat capacity (gas)** | 28.836 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ | | **Enthalpy of formation (ΔH°f)** | 0 kJ mol⁻¹ (by definition for elemental form) | | **Entropy (S°)** | 130.68 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ | | **Gibbs free energy of formation (ΔG°f)** | 0 kJ mol⁻¹ | | **Ionization energy** | 13.598 eV (first) | | **Electron affinity** | 72.8 kJ mol⁻¹ | | **Electronegativity (Pauling)** | 2.20 | | **Covalent radius** | 31 pm | | **Van der Waals radius** | 120 pm | | **Diffusion coefficient** | ~0.1 cm² s⁻¹ (high diffusivity) | | **Flammability** | Extremely flammable; explosive limits: 4 %–75 % in air | | **Reactivity** | Forms hydrides with metals; reacts with halogens, oxygen, nitrogen oxides, etc. | | **Bonding** | Diatomic (H₂) at ambient conditions; forms covalent bonds in most compounds | | **Acidic behavior** | Acts as a Lewis base (donates electron pair) in many reactions; forms acids like HCl, H₂SO₄, HNO₃ when combined with oxygen or other oxidizers | | **Role in water** | Constituent of H₂O; participates in hydrogen bonding (strong dipole-dipole interactions) | | **Industrial uses** | • Ammonia synthesis (Haber process)
• Petroleum refining (hydrocracking, hydrodesulfurization)
• Hydrogenation of fats & oils
• Production of methanol, ammonia, hydrogen peroxide, etc.
• Fuel cells (electrochemical conversion to electricity)
• Rocket propellant (liquid hydrogen + liquid oxygen)
• Metallurgical processes (reducing agent) | | **Biological relevance** | Essential for life: part of organic molecules, enzymes, metabolic pathways; involved in proton gradients (ATP synthesis) | | **Astrophysical significance** | Most abundant element in the universe (~75 % by mass); fuels stellar fusion (proton–proton chain, CNO cycle) | | **Safety considerations** | Highly flammable; requires proper ventilation; tritium is radioactive and must be handled with care | --- ### Quick Summary - **Lightest element**: one proton, one electron. - **Diatomic gas**: H₂ at room temperature. - **Low boiling/melting points**: remains gaseous under normal conditions. - **High ionization energy**: strong attraction for its single electron. - **Highly reactive**: forms a wide variety of compounds (hydrides, acids, organics). - **Key industrial & biological roles**: fuels, feedstock, catalyst, component of water and organic chemistry. - **Isotopic variants**: protium (stable), deuterium (stable, used in heavy water), tritium (radioactive, used in nuclear fusion research). Feel free to ask if you’d like more detail on any specific property or application!
